analysis.one_liner: Closes a Clean Water Act loophole so stormwater runoff from oil, gas, and mining sites needs a pollution permit.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 18, 2025, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its water subcommittee, and has not received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The FRESHER Act removes a provision in the Clean Water Act that currently bars the EPA from requiring a water pollution permit for collected, uncontaminated stormwater that runs off oil, gas, and mining operations. With the loophole closed, the EPA could require these sites to get National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits, the same requirement most industrial polluters already face. It also directs the Interior Department to study where stormwater runoff from oil and gas operations may be contaminating land, groundwater, and aquifers, and to report back to Congress within a year.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near oil, gas, and mining operations, including communities whose drinking water comes from groundwater and aquifers that stormwater runoff can carry contaminants into. All water users benefit indirectly from a rule that treats these sites like other industrial polluters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near oil, gas, and mining sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the section of the Clean Water Act (Section 402(l)(2)) that prohibits the EPA from requiring an NPDES permit for discharges of collected, uncontaminated stormwater from mining and oil and gas operations, restoring EPA's ability to require permits for those discharges.

It directs the Secretary of the Interior to study stormwater runoff from oil and gas operations in areas that may be contaminated, including analysis of measurable contamination, groundwater resources, and the susceptibility of aquifers to contamination, with a report to Congress within one year of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas operators and mining companies, which would face permitting requirements, monitoring, and pollution controls for stormwater at their sites if the EPA chooses to require permits. Some of those compliance costs could be passed to consumers through energy prices.

drawbacks.text: New permitting requirements could raise compliance costs for oil, gas, and mining operators, and some of those costs could be passed on to consumers through higher energy and mineral prices. The bill does not itself require any permits; it only restores EPA's authority to require them.

The exemption the bill strikes applies only to collected stormwater that is uncontaminated, so the practical effect depends entirely on how the EPA uses its restored authority, and a future administration could decline to write the permits.
The study provision produces only a report to Congress one year after enactment; it does not by itself change any rule or stop any contamination.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but modest: the bill restores a regulatory tool rather than imposing any new rule itself, so its value depends on EPA follow-through. The compliance costs fall on a concentrated industry, and any pass-through to consumers is likely small compared with the water-protection value in contaminated areas. The main design weakness is that the study provision delays action: it reports a year after enactment without mandating any change.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to its Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it sits with no hearing or vote scheduled and the Congress still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the FRESHER Act of 2025 in the House on November 18, 2025, joined by 21 Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on the day it was introduced.
On November 29, 2025, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action appears in the record.

The bill would strike the Clean Water Act provision that bars the EPA from requiring pollution permits for collected, uncontaminated stormwater runoff from mining and oil and gas operations, and would direct an Interior Department study of contamination, groundwater, and aquifer susceptibility.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and mining operators, who for now avoid any new federal permitting requirement for stormwater runoff at their sites. Communities near those operations gain nothing yet, because no permit requirement exists and none is on track to be created.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair has not scheduled a markup or vote
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond referring the bill to its Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment on November 29, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee has not moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill restores the EPA's authority to require pollution permits for stormwater runoff at oil and gas sites, which the industry has been exempt from since the exemption was written into the Clean Water Act. Permitting and monitoring would be a new cost, but it applies the same rule most industrial polluters already follow and protects nearby water supplies.

The same exemption covers mining operations, so miners would also face potential stormwater permitting requirements. The cost falls on a concentrated industry while the benefit is cleaner water for surrounding communities.

industries.industry: Water utilities and public water systems
industries.note: Reducing runoff contamination from oil, gas, and mining sites means less contamination reaching surface water and aquifers that public water systems draw from, lowering treatment burdens and contamination risk for ratepayers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in a subcommittee with no hearing, no Republican cosponsors, and no movement from a committee chair usually die when the Congress ends. With Republicans holding 223 of 435 House seats and the bill's support entirely Democratic, the most likely path is no further action unless the bill is attached to larger legislation.
